title: Myanmar will not fully comply with World Court's genocide orders, says Min Aung Hlaing
dek: In his first public remarks since the ICJ found Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, the president said his government would reject requirements it considers 'inappropriate'. About 1.2 million Rohingya remain in camps in Bangladesh.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Myanmar's president, Min Aung Hlaing, has said his government will not fully comply with the orders of the International Court of Justice (ICJ), which ruled a week ago that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya in 2017. It is the first public response from the man who commanded the army during those operations and now leads the country.

Speaking at a meeting on Wednesday, Min Aung Hlaing said Myanmar would take actions appropriate for a responsible country but would not comply with requirements it considered inappropriate, according to state media as cited in reports. He said the term "genocide" had damaged the country's reputation. He did not say which of the court's orders he regarded as inappropriate.

## What the court ordered

On 19 November the ICJ found, in the case brought by The Gambia in 2019 under the 1948 Genocide Convention, that Myanmar's security forces had committed genocide during the "clearance operations" in northern Rakhine State in 2017. It was the first time the court had found a state responsible for genocide. The judges also found that Myanmar had failed to prevent and punish genocide and had breached the court's January 2020 order to preserve evidence.

The court ordered Myanmar to end continuing breaches of the convention, to investigate and prosecute those suspected of involvement, to give guarantees of non-repetition, to allow the safe and voluntary return of Rohingya refugees, to pay compensation and provide rehabilitation, and to report back within two years on what it has done, according to reports. The ruling is final and cannot be appealed, but the court has no means of its own to enforce it.

Myanmar's foreign ministry has said the 2017 operations were "not carried out with genocidal intent but instead were limited in scope and duration, lasting only a matter of days", according to reports. The army has always said it was responding to attacks on police posts by the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army.

## Background

More than 730,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh after the 2017 operations, according to reports, and about 1.2 million now live in camps around Cox's Bazar. Min Aung Hlaing led the army then, seized power in a coup in February 2021, and was installed as president in April this year. As president he has been received in Thailand, Cambodia, Laos and Vietnam, according to reports.

After the ruling, Bangladesh's foreign ministry said Myanmar was "now legally bound to comply fully" and that repatriation "remains the only viable solution". Britain expelled Myanmar's defence attaché and called for an urgent Security Council meeting, according to reports. China's foreign ministry later warned the court against "overreach" and defended the vote of its judge.

## Why it matters for India and Bengal

If the orders on return and protection are not carried out, the Rohingya are likely to stay in Bangladesh for years more, adding to the strain on a neighbour already in political turmoil, and keeping pressure on the India-Bangladesh border, much of which runs along West Bengal. India borders Myanmar and is building the Kaladan transit project from Kolkata by sea to Sittwe port in Rakhine and on to Mizoram, through land now contested between the army and the Arakan Army, which controls much of the territory the Rohingya fled. India has not commented publicly on the judgment.

## What happens next

If Myanmar does not comply, The Gambia can ask the UN Security Council to act under the UN Charter, which the council has never done for an ICJ judgment; China and Russia, both close to Myanmar's military, hold vetoes. A separate phase of the case will decide the amount and form of compensation. Myanmar's first report to the court is due within two years.
